summary: New Zealand's national position on the roof rat (ship rat, Rattus rattus) is more permissive than its pest reputation suggests, though it varies by region and import is barred. The Ministry for Primary Industries confirmed in writing (June 2026) that Rattus rattus is NOT listed as an unwanted organism or a notifiable organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993, so there are no national restrictions on keeping or breeding the species under that Act, and the Animal Welfare Act 1999 requires no permit to keep, breed, or sell rats. At the national level, keeping a captive-bred roof rat is therefore legal. The catch is regional: some regional councils list Rattus rattus in their regional pest management plans, with rules that vary by region. MPI specifically noted that the Northland Regional Council plan has rules preventing the breeding or selling of Rattus rattus, and that the Auckland plan's Hauraki Gulf island rules (for example Waiheke Island) may impose restrictions. Check your own regional pest management plan (searchable on MPI's Established Pests Portal); these plans are updated roughly every ten years. Import is the firm barrier: MPI confirmed pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand, so a roof rat must be sourced domestically. Rattus rattus remains an ecological pest and a Predator Free 2050 eradication target, so never release one, secure it against escape, and do not move it into a controlled area such as the Hauraki Gulf.
agency_confirmations: Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI), Animal Welfare Team, written reply June 2026: there are NO registration or permit requirements under the Animal Welfare Act 1999 for people keeping, breeding, or selling rats (only the Act's general welfare duties and codes of welfare apply; there is no pet-rat-specific code of welfare). MPI also confirmed that pet rats CANNOT be imported into New Zealand (per MPI's 'Bringing pets to NZ other than cats and dogs' guidance). Note: this welfare-team reply addressed only the Animal Welfare Act layer; the Biosecurity Act 1993 status of the ship rat (Rattus rattus) is addressed in the confirmation below, where MPI confirmed it is NOT a national unwanted or notifiable organism.

Some regional councils list Rattus rattus in their regional pest management plans with rules that vary by region; MPI specifically noted that the Northland Regional Council plan has rules preventing the breeding or selling of Rattus rattus, and that the Auckland plan's Hauraki Gulf island rules (for example Waiheke Island) may impose restrictions. Regional plans are searchable on MPI's New Zealand Established Pests Portal and are updated roughly every ten years.

keep.why: MPI confirmed in writing (June 2026) that Rattus rattus is not an unwanted or notifiable organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993, so there is no national Biosecurity restriction on keeping it, and the Animal Welfare Act 1999 requires no permit to keep a rat. Keeping a captive-bred roof rat is therefore legal at the national level. Regional pest management plans can add local rules, so check your regional plan, but mere private keeping of a securely contained animal is generally allowed. The general Animal Welfare Act duties apply, and the animal must never be released or allowed to escape.
keep.governing_law: Biosecurity Act 1993 (R. rattus is NOT an unwanted/notifiable organism, MPI June 2026, so no national keeping restriction); Animal Welfare Act 1999 (general duties, no keeping permit); regional pest management plans (local variation).

breed.why: Legal nationally: MPI confirmed (June 2026) there are no national restrictions on breeding Rattus rattus under the Biosecurity Act, and the Animal Welfare Act requires no breeding permit. But it is restricted in some regions. MPI specifically flagged that the Northland Regional Council pest management plan has rules preventing the breeding (and selling) of Rattus rattus, and that Auckland's Hauraki Gulf island rules may restrict it. So breeding is allowed nationally but can be prohibited in particular regions. Check your regional pest management plan (searchable on MPI's Established Pests Portal) before breeding.
breed.governing_law: Biosecurity Act 1993 (no NATIONAL breeding restriction, MPI June 2026); regional pest management plans (Northland prevents breeding/selling; Auckland Hauraki Gulf islands may restrict); Animal Welfare Act 1999 (no breeding permit).

sell_give.why: Legal nationally (no national Biosecurity or Animal Welfare restriction on selling rats, MPI June 2026), but restricted in some regions: the Northland Regional Council pest management plan prevents the selling of Rattus rattus, and other regional plans may too. Check your regional pest management plan before selling or rehoming. No national dealer licence applies.
sell_give.governing_law: Biosecurity Act 1993 (no national sale restriction, MPI June 2026); regional pest management plans (Northland prevents selling); Animal Welfare Act 1999 (no dealer permit).

transport.why: Importing a pet rat into New Zealand is prohibited: MPI confirmed (June 2026) that pet rats cannot be imported, and there is no pet-rodent import health standard, so a roof rat must be sourced domestically. Domestic movement of a lawfully held animal is otherwise fine, but do not move a rat into a regional controlled area such as Auckland's Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area near pest-free islands, and meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare. Never release a rat: it is a Predator Free 2050 eradication target.
transport.governing_law: MPI import guidance (pet rats not importable, June 2026); regional controlled-area movement rules (e.g. Auckland Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area); Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare 2018.

restrictions.summary: Pet rats cannot be imported into New Zealand (MPI, June 2026). There is no pet pathway and no pet-rodent import health standard, so a roof rat must be sourced domestically. Do not move a rat into a regional controlled area such as Auckland's Hauraki Gulf Controlled Area, and meet the Animal Welfare (Transport within New Zealand) Code of Welfare for any internal transport. Never release a rat.

restrictions.summary: Check your REGIONAL pest management plan. R. rattus is not restricted nationally (MPI, June 2026), but some regional councils restrict it. The Northland Regional Council plan has rules preventing the breeding or selling of Rattus rattus, and Auckland's Hauraki Gulf island rules (e.g. Waiheke) may restrict it. Search Rattus rattus on MPI's New Zealand Established Pests Portal to find your region's rules; plans are updated roughly every ten years. Secure the animal against escape and never release it.
steps: Search 'Rattus rattus' on MPI's Established Pests Portal to find your region's status and plan
Read your regional council's pest management plan for any breeding/selling/keeping rules
In Northland (and possibly Auckland's Hauraki Gulf islands), do not breed or sell R. rattus
Keep the animal securely contained; never release it

restrictions.summary: Keepers owe the Animal Welfare Act 1999 duties (meet the animal's physical, health, and behavioural needs and treat sickness or injury). There is no code of welfare specific to pet rats, but the general duties apply.
